lessons.title: নেওয়া (neowā) — "to take," and the verb that finishes other verbs
lessons.gloss: to take — and the verb that finishes other verbs

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page

segments.text: Bengali rarely leaves a verb standing alone. This is the verb it props most of them up with — and the tail it wears will look familiar.
নেওয়া — neowā — to take.
আমি নিই (āmi nii), "I take." আপনি নেন (āpni nen), respectfully.

নেওয়া (neowā) is নে (ne) + ওয়া (-owā). ন is a dental n, tongue on the teeth. The ওয়া tail is the one every dictionary-form verb of this kind wears — you have it already on হওয়া, যাওয়া and খাওয়া.

নেওয়া (neowā) is Sanskrit √নী (√nī), "to lead, to carry away." It is a well-attested Indo-Iranian root — Avestan nayeiti, "he leads"; Sanskrit netṛ, "a leader," which is why a politician in Kolkata or Delhi is a netā. Beyond that branch the trail thins, and English kept nothing from it. No cousin will be manufactured for you here; some roots stayed home.
The lesson worth more than a cousin is what Bengali does with the verb.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the verb that ends a compound

segments.text: Put a verb into its -এ form (likhe, "having written"; niye, "having taken") and hang a second verb behind it. The second verb stops meaning what it means and starts colouring the first:

utterances: compound: লিখে নেওয়া (likhe neowā). what it does: write it down — take the writing for yourself.
compound: নিয়ে আসা (niye āsā). what it does: bring — come, having taken.
compound: নিয়ে যাওয়া (niye jāwā). what it does: take away — go, having taken.

segments.text: Bengali has no separate word for "bring." It has "come having taken." And নেওয়া is a noun as readily as লেখা was: দেওয়া-নেওয়া (deowā-neowā), "giving-and-taking," is the everyday word for dealings between people.

segments.instruction: the same tail four times — "hôwā, jāwā, khāwā, neowā"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the same tail four times — "hôwā, jāwā, khāwā, neowā"]

segments.instruction: bring, then take away — "niye āsā … niye jāwā"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: bring, then take away — "niye āsā … niye jāwā"]

segments.text: How does Bengali say "bring," having no word for it? (নিয়ে আসা — "come having taken"; and "take away" is নিয়ে যাওয়া.) Does English share নেওয়া (neowā)'s root? (No — √nī stayed in Indo-Iranian, and that is the honest answer.) Name two more Bengali verbs that are also nouns. (লেখা "a piece of writing" and দেখা "a seeing" — every -া form does it.)

lessons.title: জিজ্ঞাসা করা (jijñāsā kôrā) — "to ask," which is wanting to know
lessons.gloss: to ask — literally "to do a wanting-to-know," and the door into a thousand verbs

segments.text: Chapter 7 warned you about a knot of letters, then spared you it. Here it is, inside a word you will use daily — and the word is Chapter 7's verb with an appetite.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: জিজ্ঞাসা করা

segments.text: জিজ্ঞাসা করা — jijñāsā kôrā — to ask.
আমি জিজ্ঞাসা করি (āmi jiggāshā kôri), "I ask" — two words, one verb.

জিজ্ঞাসা is জি + জ্ঞা + সা. The middle piece জ্ঞ is the knot of জ and ঞ Chapter 7 named on √jñā — and Bengali never says jñ. It says gg, so the spelled jijñāsā is spoken jiggāshā, with the s becomes sh tilt at the end.
জিজ্ঞাসা is Sanskrit's desiderative of √জ্ঞা (√jñā, "to know") — the form meaning wanting to do a thing. Jijñāsati is "he desires to know"; jijñāsā is the desire itself. Bengali took the noun.

So asking is not a separate idea here. It is জানা with an appetite — and the root behind both is the one Chapter 7 traced: PIE ǵneh₃-, English know, Latin nōscere (notice), Greek gnôsis (diagnosis). The doubled ji- is the desiderative's signature: a quiet echo of the root, meaning reaching for it.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: any noun plus করা is a verb

utterances: noun: কাজ (kāj), work. noun + করা: কাজ করা — to work.
noun: জিজ্ঞাসা (jijñāsā), a wanting-to-know. noun + করা: জিজ্ঞাসা করা (jijñāsā kôrā) — to ask.

segments.text: Chapter 5 built kāj kôrā this way. It is more than a compound: it is the way Bengali makes verbs. The stock of true verbs is small and closed, while nouns pour in from Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic and English — each becoming a verb the moment করা stands behind it. Learn a noun, learn a verb.
Last lesson’s compound stacks on top: জিজ্ঞাসা করে নেওয়া (jijñāsā kôre neowā) — "just go ahead and ask."

segments.text: How does Bengali say জ্ঞ, and what is জিজ্ঞাসা literally? (gg, never jñ; and a wanting-to-know, the desiderative of জানা's root.) Someone asks whether you know their brother — which knowing verb answers? (চেনা — a person is known by acquaintance; জানা is for facts.) How do you make a verb from a noun you met this morning? (Put করা behind it.)

lessons.title: সাহায্য করা (sāhājjo kôrā) — "to help," which is going along with someone
lessons.gloss: to help — "to go together with," and the word that finally shows you the inherent vowel

segments.text: Chapter 6 said Bengali's inherent vowel leans to o, then admitted it could not show you. This word can — and it is the word you will most want when stuck.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: সাহায্য করা

segments.text: সাহায্য করা — sāhājjo kôrā — to help.
আমাকে সাহায্য করুন (āmāke sāhājjo kôrun), "please help me"; āmāke is "to me."
সাহায্য is সা + হা + য্য. The last piece is য stacked on itself — a conjunct, how Bengali writes a doubled consonant.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: a doubled letter, and a vowel nobody writes

segments.text: Two rules land at the end, neither a quirk. Bengali reads a doubled য as jj, not yy. And nothing is written after it, so it takes the inherent vowel, which leans to o: sāhājjo, never sāhājja.
Chapter 6 could not show that inherent o in ek, dui, tin, chār, pā̃ch, since none of the five ends in a bare consonant. This one does. সা takes the s becomes sh tilt, so the whole is shāhājjo.
সাহায্য is Sanskrit sāhāyya, "companionship," on সহায় (sahāya), "a companion" — which is সহ- (saha-), "together," plus √ই (√i), "to go." A helper goes along with you.

Both halves have secure English cousins. Saha- is PIE sem-, "together": English same, Greek homós (homogeneous), Latin similis (similar). √i is PIE h₁ey-, "to go": Latin īre gives exit and transit; Greek ión gives ion. So "help" is same-going, and English holds the pieces without ever building the word.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: asking for help is where the respect ladder bites

segments.text: Another noun + করা, like জিজ্ঞাসা করা (jijñāsā kôrā). The respect sits where Chapter 7 put it — in করা’s ending:

utterances: who you are asking: তুই (tui, intimate). "help": সাহায্য কর (kôr).
who you are asking: তুমি (tumi, familiar). "help": সাহায্য করো (kôro).
who you are asking: আপনি (āpni, respectful). "help": সাহায্য করুন (kôrun).

segments.text: Say kôr to a stranger and you were not rude by accident, but in grammar.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: the ladder — "sāhājjo kôr … kôro … kôrun"]
[YOU SAY: please help me — "āmāke sāhājjo kôrun"]

segments.text: Why does সাহায্য end in -o with nothing written there? (The inherent vowel — the thing the five numbers could not show.) Which form to a stranger? (করুন — kôr is for তুই.) What is a sahāya? (One who goes with you.)

segments.text: Every verb so far has let you be the one doing it. Here is one that does not.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: ভালো লাগা

segments.text: ভালো লাগা — bhālo lāgā — to like.
আমার ভালো লাগে (āmār bhālo lāge), "I like it." Not āmi — āmār, "to me."
ভালো is yours from Chapter 3. The new half is লাগা: লা + গা, গ being a hard g as in go.
লাগা is Sanskrit √লগ্ (√lag), "to attach, to stick": āmār bhālo lāge says, literally, "good sticks to me."

ভালোবাসা (bhālobāsā), "to love," is ভালো plus বাসা, a verb no longer used alone. Its origin is genuinely disputed; the commonest proposal is Sanskrit √বস্ (√vas), "to dwell" — love as housed in goodness. If so it carries a startling cousin, since √vas is PIE h₂wes-, "to stay," which became Old English wesan and so English was. That "if" is real, and stays open.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: liking lands on you; loving you do

utterances: Bengali: আমার ভালো লাগে. word for word: to-me good sticks — I like it.
Bengali: আমার চা ভালো লাগে. word for word: to-me tea good sticks — I like tea.
Bengali: আমি ভালোবাসি. word for word: I love.

segments.text: That āmār … shape is how Bengali says I have — আমার … আছে, with আছে carrying the weight and no future of its own to give.

ভালোবাসা breaks the pattern on purpose: āmi bhālobāsi puts you in the subject's chair. It is a noun too — "love" itself — as লেখা was "a piece of writing." One form serves everybody. The harmony has nothing to bite on: bāsi and bāse keep their ā.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "āmār bhālo lāge" — hearing "to me," not "I"]

segments.instruction: I like tea — "āmār chā bhālo lāge" — the tea Bengali eats, "chā khāwā"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: I like tea — "āmār chā bhālo lāge" — the tea Bengali eats, "chā khāwā"]

segments.instruction: the eight verbs of these two chapters — "bhābā, bojhā, pôṛā, lekhā, neowā, jijñāsā kôrā, sāhājjo kôrā, bhālo lāgā"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the eight verbs of these two chapters — "bhābā, bojhā, pôṛā, lekhā, neowā, jijñāsā kôrā, sāhājjo kôrā, bhālo lāgā"]

segments.text: Who is the subject of āmār bhālo lāge, and what else is built that way? (Not you — the good is; আমার … আছে, "I have," and আছে has no future of its own to give.) Does āmi bhālobāsi behave the same, and would a woman say it differently? (No, and no — loving takes you as subject; Bengali has no grammatical gender.) Name two verbs that are also nouns. (ভালোবাসা "love," লেখা "writing.") Why bāsi, not bosi? (Nothing to raise — this stem has ā.)
